canonical_definition:
What it is. Across the papers, PIQA is most commonly described as Physical Interaction: Question Answering, a benchmark or dataset for physical commonsense reasoning about everyday situations, objects, and interactions. The prevailing format is multiple-choice question answering, often framed as choosing between two candidate solutions or selecting the most physically plausible action or solution; one paper describes 21k questions across different subsets. A few papers sharpen this as grounded physical world understanding or goal-driven questions, while isolated descriptions label it Physical Interaction Quality Assessment.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PIQA to 13 constructs and 12 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures Commonsense reasoning, with additional papers using it for Reasoning and Physical world understanding; on the behavioral side, the most recurrent indicators are Language understanding task performance and Zero-shot question answering. Claims therefore cluster around physical commonsense and reasoning, but they also spread to 10 other constructs and 10 other behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. Across the literature, PIQA is usually one item in larger downstream evaluation suites rather than a standalone instrument, most often reported as zero-shot accuracy alongside other commonsense benchmarks, especially HellaSwag and WinoGrande. A smaller line uses it in few-shot or generalization settings, including 5-shot and 10-shot evaluations, and a few papers place it in generative QA or grounding-oriented evaluation. It is also linked to 3 evaluation instruments, most often lm-evaluation-harness, then OpenCompass and OLMES, which papers use as standardized tools or benchmark suites for running PIQA evaluations.

Concerns raised. Papers use PIQA in analyses of benchmark overfitting and in-context learning: one paper evaluates the impact of data contamination on a mixed benchmark set that includes PiQA, and one paper reports that PIQA shows minimal benefits across all models in an in-context learning comparison.

characterization_sections.label: What it is.
characterization_sections.text: Across the papers, PIQA is most commonly described as Physical Interaction: Question Answering, a benchmark or dataset for physical commonsense reasoning about everyday situations, objects, and interactions. The prevailing format is multiple-choice question answering, often framed as choosing between two candidate solutions or selecting the most physically plausible action or solution; one paper describes 21k questions across different subsets. A few papers sharpen this as grounded physical world understanding or goal-driven questions, while isolated descriptions label it Physical Interaction Quality Assessment.

characterization_sections.label: What it is claimed to measure.
characterization_sections.text: Papers link PIQA to 13 constructs and 12 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures Commonsense reasoning, with additional papers using it for Reasoning and Physical world understanding; on the behavioral side, the most recurrent indicators are Language understanding task performance and Zero-shot question answering. Claims therefore cluster around physical commonsense and reasoning, but they also spread to 10 other constructs and 10 other behavioral indicators.

characterization_sections.label: Space of uses.
characterization_sections.text: Across the literature, PIQA is usually one item in larger downstream evaluation suites rather than a standalone instrument, most often reported as zero-shot accuracy alongside other commonsense benchmarks, especially HellaSwag and WinoGrande. A smaller line uses it in few-shot or generalization settings, including 5-shot and 10-shot evaluations, and a few papers place it in generative QA or grounding-oriented evaluation. It is also linked to 3 evaluation instruments, most often lm-evaluation-harness, then OpenCompass and OLMES, which papers use as standardized tools or benchmark suites for running PIQA evaluations.

characterization_sections.label: Concerns raised.
characterization_sections.text: Papers use PIQA in analyses of benchmark overfitting and in-context learning: one paper evaluates the impact of data contamination on a mixed benchmark set that includes PiQA, and one paper reports that PIQA shows minimal benefits across all models in an in-context learning comparison.

characterization:
What it is. Across the papers, PIQA is most commonly described as Physical Interaction: Question Answering, a benchmark or dataset for physical commonsense reasoning about everyday situations, objects, and interactions. The prevailing format is multiple-choice question answering, often framed as choosing between two candidate solutions or selecting the most physically plausible action or solution; one paper describes 21k questions across different subsets. A few papers sharpen this as grounded physical world understanding or goal-driven questions, while isolated descriptions label it Physical Interaction Quality Assessment.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PIQA to 13 constructs and 12 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures Commonsense reasoning, with additional papers using it for Reasoning and Physical world understanding; on the behavioral side, the most recurrent indicators are Language understanding task performance and Zero-shot question answering. Claims therefore cluster around physical commonsense and reasoning, but they also spread to 10 other constructs and 10 other behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. Across the literature, PIQA is usually one item in larger downstream evaluation suites rather than a standalone instrument, most often reported as zero-shot accuracy alongside other commonsense benchmarks, especially HellaSwag and WinoGrande. A smaller line uses it in few-shot or generalization settings, including 5-shot and 10-shot evaluations, and a few papers place it in generative QA or grounding-oriented evaluation. It is also linked to 3 evaluation instruments, most often lm-evaluation-harness, then OpenCompass and OLMES, which papers use as standardized tools or benchmark suites for running PIQA evaluations.

Concerns raised. Papers use PIQA in analyses of benchmark overfitting and in-context learning: one paper evaluates the impact of data contamination on a mixed benchmark set that includes PiQA, and one paper reports that PIQA shows minimal benefits across all models in an in-context learning comparison.
